titre_video: 70 Cents of Every Dollar Is Over: The Collapse of American Defense Dominance

segments.titre: Canada's economic trap after the break with the US
segments.resume: The video opens with Canada caught in an economic trap: after 80 years of close ties, trade talks collapsed and tariffs forced Prime Minister Mark Carney to sever military and trade ties. Every pipeline, trainline and shipping route points south, so Canada's push for independence handed America a kill switch, though Washington has not yet retaliated.
segments.texte: Canada has just walked into a vicious economic trap. For 80 years, the relationship between the U.S. and Canada seemed unbreakable. Now, tensions are brewing and trade talks have collapsed. A brutal volley of tariffs has forced Prime Minister Mark Carney to draw a line in the sand. Canada will not be held hostage. Military and trade ties have been completely severed. But there’s one problem. Every pipeline, trainline and shipping route points south. Canada wanted economic independence. Instead, they gave America the kill switch. And the worst part? Washington hasn’t even retaliated… yet.

segments.titre: Geography created wealth and a structural illusion
segments.resume: Living next to the most powerful military and economy on Earth brought Canada staggering benefits, largely because of geography. The same geography created a dangerous structural illusion.
segments.texte: Living next door to the most powerful military and economy on Earth, meant Canada reaped staggering benefits. Geography made most of that wealth possible. But it also created something far more complicated: A dangerous structural illusion.

segments.titre: Canada and the US: the world's largest bilateral trade relationship
segments.resume: By 2025 the US took over three-quarters of Canadian goods exports and supplied almost half its imports, a relationship worth over $900 billion. Canada sends precious metals, vehicles, nuclear reactors and oddities like wigs and dog muzzles, and receives machinery, electronics, plastics and pet food, leaving its economy hardwired into the US market.
segments.texte: By 2025, the U.S. accounted for over three-quarters of Canadian exports of goods, while supplying almost half of its imports. It’s worth over $900 billion, making it the largest bilateral trading relationship in the world. Every single year Canada has pumped tens of billions of dollars into the U.S. through heavy hitters like precious metals, vehicles and nuclear reactors. But away from the headlines, obscure items like wigs, egg-grading equipment, and dog muzzles have steadily flowed south into vast, lucrative markets. And America reciprocates. Billions of dollars’ worth machinery, electronics and plastics move north. There’s also millions of smaller items like pet food and fries. Canada’s economy has become hardwired into the U.S. market. It relies on it to survive.it. And

segments.titre: Energy: Canada's most critical dependency
segments.resume: In 2025 Canada exported 6.5 million barrels per day of hydrocarbons, with the US taking 90.8 percent, nearly two thirds of US crude imports and close to 100 percent of imported natural gas. Pipelines, power lines, rail and shipping corridors make sudden decoupling seem almost physically impossible.
segments.texte: that dependency is most critical in one sector. Energy. In 2025, Canada exported 6.5 million barrels per day of hydrocarbons globally. The U.S. to the bulk of that, taking a massive 90.8%. That supply makes up nearly two thirds of all the crude oil and close to 100% of all the natural gas imported by the U.S. Dozens of pipelines, power lines, and a web of rail and shipping corridors lock the countries together. It’s a structural integration at a level that makes sudden decoupling almost physically impossible. Or so you’d think.

segments.titre: Trade talks collapse: Canada's account
segments.resume: In late August 2026 trade talks collapsed and both sides blamed each other. Carney said America asked too much and offered too little, and Canadian officials said the US blocked heavy trucks from tariff relief, reneged on aluminum and steel tariff cuts, wanted control over Canada's steel tariffs and a veto over future free-trade agreements.
segments.texte: Because Mark Carney just filed for economic divorce. In late August 2026, after months of escalating tensions, trade talks collapsed. Both sides are pointing the finger of blame at each other. Carney said that “[America] asked too much, and they offered too little.” According to him, the U.S. pulled a last minute bait and switch, introducing “unfair [and] uneconomic” terms. Canadian officials claimed the U.S. had blocked heavy trucks from tariff relief, reneged on a deal to slash tariffs on Canadian aluminum and steel. But that’s not all. They said the U.S. wanted to control Canada’s steel tariffs with other countries, and even floated the idea of having a veto over Canada’s future free-trade agreements. The U.S. sees things differently.

segments.titre: Trade talks collapse: Washington's account
segments.resume: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Canada backed out of terms agreed earlier that week and walked back other commitments, adding that Canada wanted more. Vice President JD Vance accused Canada of unreasonable last-minute demands, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Canada blew up a nearly complete deal for political reasons.
segments.texte: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that Canada had backed out of terms they had already “agreed earlier [in the] week”. He also added that Canada has walked back on other commitments. Later, in an interview with CNBC, he put it more bluntly: “They wanted more.” The rest of Washington fell into line. Vice President JD Vance accused Canada of bringing “unreasonable last-minute demands” and were trying to “take advantage of America.” By early September, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick claimed Canada “blew up” a nearly complete deal “for political reasons.”

segments.titre: The US list of grievances against Canada
segments.resume: Behind the rhetoric, the US lists complaints: Canada banned US alcohol in 8 of 10 provinces, auto tariffs lingering from the 2025 tariff war, and protected dairy policies. Both sides had serious concerns, and resolving them required patience and real diplomacy between long-term allies.
segments.texte: Behind the rhetoric, the U.S. has a massive list of complaints. Canada banned U.S. alcohol in 8 out of 10 Canadian provinces. Auto tariffs that were lingering from the original U.S./Canadian tariff war from 2025. And Canada’s notorious protected dairy policies. Both sides had serious issues and concerns. Resolving them required skill, patience, and actual diplomacy. Something that two long term allies could figure out, right?

segments.titre: The US imposes 50 percent tariffs on C$20 billion of Canadian goods
segments.resume: Washington slapped 50 percent tariffs on CAD$20 billion of Canadian exports, including wine, furniture, dairy, cement, clothing and sporting goods. Even Canadian wigs and articles for Christmas festivities were hit.
segments.texte: Wrong. Washington detonated a grenade. The administration slapped 50% tariffs on CAD$20 billion of exports, including wine, furniture, dairy, cement, clothing and sporting goods. Even the Canadian wigs got hit, as well as “articles for Christmas festivities,” and a host of other eclectic and often exotic products.

segments.titre: Canada's counter-tariffs and the inflation cost
segments.resume: Carney responded with counter-tariffs of 15 to 50 percent on roughly $20 billion of US goods, effective just after midnight on September 8, with iron, steel and aluminum almost half the list plus plastics, electrical machinery, furniture and cosmetics. The tit-for-tat tariffs hit consumers and businesses and are inflationary, eroding purchasing power.
segments.texte: Carney hit straight back. Counter-tariffs of 15 to 50% were applied to roughly $20 billion of U.S. goods and took effect just after midnight on September 8th. Iron, steel, and aluminum products make up almost half of the list, a direct mirror to the U.S. tariffs that started this economic death spiral. Canada is also targeting other “big ticket” items like plastics, electrical machinery, furniture, and cosmetics. Because the tit-for-tat tariffs are so far-reaching, they’re going to hammer ordinary consumers and businesses of all sizes. Tariffs are inflationary. They act like a sponge, absorbing the purchasing power right out of your money. But there was something else lurking in the background. A shadow hanging over this entire trade war.

segments.titre: Carney's pledge: 70 cents of every defense dollar to the US is over
segments.resume: Carney wants to cut defense spending with America; Canada's push to reduce reliance on US defense suppliers added fuel to the August breakdown, though it was not publicly blamed. At the Liberal Party convention in April 2026 he declared the days of sending 70 cents of every military dollar to the US are over, as over 70 percent of Canada's military capital spending flows to US suppliers.
segments.texte: Carney wants to slash defense spending with America. While it wasn’t publicly blamed for the breakdown of the August talks, Canada's push to reduce its dependence on U.S. defense suppliers added serious fuel to the fire. That single move threatens to tank the Canadian dollar, and leave the country vulnerable. It all traces back to April 2026, and the Liberal Party’s national convention. Mark Carney stood before delegates and declared: “The days of our military sending 70 cents of every dollar to the U.S. are over.” It was a standing-ovation moment. While it was a fiery speech, Carney was also outlining a radical transformation of Canadian defense policy. According to the Prime Minister’s office, over 70% of Canada’s military capital spending flows directly to U.S. suppliers. It’s been a structural reality for decades, born out of geography, convenience, and the quality of U.S. military tech. But more importantly, the implicit assumption that the U.S. would always be a reliable ally. Carney was effectively declaring that assumption DOA.

segments.titre: The Defense Industrial Strategy: 70 percent domestic contracts
segments.resume: The new Defense Industrial Strategy aims to award 70 percent of defense procurement contracts to domestic firms, grow defense industry revenues by more than 240 percent, raise defense exports by 50 percent and create up to 125,000 jobs. It is a bold vision of military sovereignty on paper but a logistical nightmare in reality.
segments.texte: But declaring independence and actually achieving it are two different things. The new Defense Industrial Strategy unveiled by Carney aims to do something radical: award 70% of defense procurement contracts to domestic firms. It also sets ambitious long-term targets, like boosting defense industry revenues by more than 240%, increasing defense exports by 50%, and creating up to 125,000 jobs. It’s a bold vision for Canadian military sovereignty… On paper. In reality, it’s a logistical nightmare.

segments.titre: Canadian defense firms are embedded in US supply chains: the Stryker
segments.resume: Nearly half of Canada's defense output is exported, 63 percent of it to the US, and many exports are made by subsidiaries of US companies. The Stryker armored vehicle, backbone of the US Army, is based on a Canadian design and built in Canada by General Dynamics Land Systems-Canada, a subsidiary of General Dynamics.
segments.texte: Nearly half of everything Canada’s defense sector builds is shipped out of the country. 63% of that went to the U.S., with small percentages going to the U.K., Australia, and New Zealand. Canadian defense firms are deeply ingrained in U.S. supply chains. In fact, many of the Canadian military exports are built by subsidiaries of U.S. companies. Take the Stryker. The legendary armored vehicle is the backbone of the U.S. army. But it’s based on a Canadian designed vehicle and made by General Dynamics Land Systems – Canada, or GDLS-C… a wholly owned subsidiary of U.S. giant General Dynamics Corporation, headquartered in Reston, Virginia. So the U.S.’s signature ground vehicle is a Canadian design, built in Canada, by an American owned company.

segments.titre: The 'Buy Canadian' policy is an illusion
segments.resume: Under Carney's Buy Canadian policy, US-owned subsidiaries count as Canadian, as with sensors and ammunition. A July 2026 report found foreign-owned companies won more than 70 percent of contracts examined, so the redirection of money is about where the invoice is written, not where profits end up.
segments.texte: There are similar dynamics at play across Canada’s other top exports, including sensors and ammunition. The irony is that under Carney’s “Buy Canadian” policy, these U.S.-owned subsidiaries are considered Canadian. A July 2026 report exposed the truth. Foreign-owned companies scooped up more than 70% of the contracts examined under the Buy Canadian policy. The entire policy is an illusion. The “redirection” of money isn’t about where the profits end up, more where the invoice is written. But while the finances are murky, the security nightmare facing Canada is clear.

segments.titre: Critical US-made equipment: River-class destroyers and C-17 airlift
segments.resume: Canada's flagship $77 billion fleet of 15 River-class destroyers has British hulls but a US-made combat system, including Aegis and Tomahawk missiles, which cannot be removed without redesigning the ship. Canada also relies on 5 C-17 Globemasters, the only aircraft able to fly a 60-ton Leopard 2 over 1,000 miles, with no viable alternative.
segments.texte: Canada imports a wide range of military equipment from the U.S., some of it critical for the nation’s security. Canada’s flagship $77 billion fleet of 15 River-class destroyers is currently under construction. The hulls are British, but their entire combat system, including the Aegis Combat System, and Tomahawk missiles, is U.S.-made. You can’t pull those systems without completely redesigning the ship It’s functionally impossible. Canada also has no viable alternatives to replace its U.S.-made strategic airlift aircraft. Canada relies on its 5 C-17 Globemasters for its strategic airlift capability. The C-17 is the only aircraft that can fly a 60-ton Leopard 2 over 1,000 miles (1,609 km). Building an equivalent would be extremely expensive and time consuming. If it could be done at all.

segments.titre: No sovereign GPS or ballistic missile defense
segments.resume: Canada has no sovereign positioning, navigation and timing capability and depends on the US GPS constellation; Europe's Galileo is no drop-in replacement for encrypted military GPS, and a Canadian version would take 15 to 20 years and tens of billions. Canada also has zero ballistic missile defense and relies entirely on Washington, so breaking away requires building a whole industrial ecosystem while exposed.
segments.texte: Even more problematic would be the loss of U.S. GPS. Canada has no sovereign positioning, navigation, or timing capability, or PNT for short. Every vehicle, aircraft, and ship depends on the U.S.’s GPS constellation. Europe’s Galileo exists, but it’s not a drop-in replacement for encrypted, military-grade American GPS. Building a Canadian version would take 15 to 20 years and cost tens of billions of dollars. Canada also has zero ballistic missile defense, or BMD. It relies entirely on Washington to intercept any incoming threats.There is no Canadian backup and no domestic capacity to build one. Slamming the door on U.S. defence isn’t as simple as building new factories. A whole industrial ecosystem has to be created. While that happens, Canada is exposed.

segments.titre: Trade war escalation threatens Canada's export-dependent economy
segments.resume: Carney's 70 cents declaration cast a shadow over the trade talks and likely contributed to their breakdown. In the first half of 2026 Canada shipped almost 68 percent of exports to the US; ports at Vancouver and Prince Rupert, pipelines, rail and integrated auto supply chains cannot redirect to new markets quickly.
segments.texte: That’s why Carney’s 70 cents defense declaration cast a toxic shadow over the recent trade talks. It also likely contributed to their breakdown. Now, the trade war escalation that has followed threatens to push the entire Canadian economy off a cliff. In the first half of 2026, Canada shipped almost 68% of its total exports to the U.S. It reinforced the reality that Canada’s export infrastructure is built for one market. If the tariff war crushes Canadian competitiveness in America, companies will have to find new markets immediately… or face economic ruin. But even if it finds customers in different parts of the world, how exactly is it going to physically supply them? The ports at Vancouver and Prince Rupert can’t handle even a fraction of the goods that flow south. The pipelines can’t reroute overnight. The rail lines don’t switch direction. And the integrated automotive supply chains can’t be untangled without years

segments.titre: Diversifying trade: US share down from 75 to 66 percent
segments.resume: Carney vowed to diversify trade away from the US, and by July 2026 the US-bound export share had dropped to 66 percent from an average of 75 percent. Doubling non-US exports over a decade needs infrastructure and trade agreements that do not exist yet, and Canada's $20 billion retaliation faces an economy 13 times its size.
segments.texte: of investment and massive disruption. Still, Carney has vowed to diversify Canada’s trade away from the U.S. And on paper, he’s made a decent start. By July 2026, the share of U.S.-bound Canadian exports had dropped to 66% from an average of 75 percent before the trade war. But that’s still a massive dependency. Doubling non-U.S. exports over the next decade, requires infrastructure that doesn’t exist, trade agreements that haven’t been signed, and customers who aren’t buying. And this is where the math gets brutal. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs cover $20 billion of U.S. goods. But Canada is picking a fight against an economy 13 times its size. That’s not a fair fight.

segments.titre: The auto industry and the threat of 50 percent tariffs in 2027
segments.resume: The North American auto industry is the poster child of cross-border supply chains, with parts crossing the border multiple times before a vehicle is finished. The Trump administration threatened to raise US tariffs on all Canadian cars, trucks and parts to 50 percent from January 1, 2027, which would be catastrophic on both sides.
segments.texte: The North American auto industry is the poster child for cross-border supply chains. Or at least it has been. Parts cross the border multiple times before a vehicle rolls off the assembly line on one side or the other. But the Trump administration has threatened to raise U.S. tariffs on all cars, trucks, and automotive parts from Canada to 50% starting January 1st, 2027. It would be catastrophic for producers on both sides of the border, not to mention consumers. Then, there’s energy.

segments.titre: Canada's energy trap: pipelines run south
segments.resume: Canada supplies 64 percent of US crude imports, but pipelines run south, refineries are in the US Midwest, and shipping capacity to Asia or Europe does not exist at scale. Shutting this down would mean job losses, supply chain disruption, reduced competitiveness and higher prices for ordinary Canadians.
segments.texte: Canada supplies 64% of all U.S. crude oil imports. While the U.S. desperately needs that energy, Canada is trapped. The pipelines run south. The refineries are in the U.S. Midwest. And the shipping capacity to export to Asia or Europe doesn’t exist at the scale required. It’s impossible to just shut this all down and skip happily over to new markets. It spells disaster for ordinary Canadians. They’ll be faced with job losses, supply chain disruptions, reduced competitiveness, and higher prices. It’s going to be painful.

segments.titre: Cutting the 70-cent defense dollar means a decade of economic pain
segments.resume: Carney's pledge is not just a geopolitical statement but a commitment to a decade or more of economic hurt in exchange for long-term sovereignty. The question is whether Canada can survive the transition.
segments.texte: So when Carney talks about cutting the 70-cent defense dollar, he’s not just making a geopolitical statement. He’s committing to a decade or more of economic hurt in exchange for long-term sovereignty. The question is whether Canada can survive the transition. To be fair, his instinct is understandable.

segments.titre: Canadians back Carney as trust in Washington erodes
segments.resume: Carney's tough stance toward Trump has majority support, with polls showing 63 to 85 percent approval after reciprocal tariffs. His government was forged under a trade war and annexation threats; the US House voted to reject certain tariffs but the President kept duties on Canadian autos, steel and aluminum using emergency powers, eroding trust.
segments.texte: His tough stance with Donald Trump seems to have the support of the majority of Canadians, despite the high potential for disaster. Polls in the days immediately after reciprocal tariffs were announced showed anywhere from 63 to 85% support for his actions. The Carney government was forged in the shadow of a trade war and threats of annexation from President Trump. While the U.S. House voted to reject certain tariffs, the President maintained a hardline stance, using emergency economic powers to justify duties on Canadian autos, steel, and aluminum. Now, trust in Washington has eroded.

segments.titre: Experts split: rupture or recalibration
segments.resume: Alistair Edgar of Wilfrid Laurier University calls it a fundamental rupture and says the US can no longer be considered a reliable ally. Erika Simpson of Western University sees recalibration rather than rupture, and acknowledges Canada is joined at the hip to the US so decoupling must be gradual.
segments.texte: That seemingly unshakeable alliance has been battered. And it's not just Canada reassessing its options. Alistair Edgar, an associate professor of political science at Wilfrid Laurier University, sees this as a “fundamental rupture”. In his words, “The U.S. can no longer be considered a reliable and trusted ally and partner,” Erika Simpson, an associate professor of international relations at Western University, offers a more measured view. According to her, Canada’s plan reflects a cautious strategic adjustment rather than a decisive break. “This should be understood as recalibration rather than rupture,” Simpson said. But even she acknowledges the difficult situation Canada is in. Economically and militarily, it is more or less joined at the hip to its southern neighbor. Any decoupling will of necessity have to be gradual. And that’s the problem.

segments.titre: Who runs out of money first? Leverage on both sides
segments.resume: Carney's rhetoric promises radical change but the transition will be slow, painful and uncertain for both countries. Canada has leverage through energy and critical minerals for the US defense industry, but as the smaller economy it has more to lose and must build domestic capacity in neglected sectors.
segments.texte: Carney’s rhetoric promises radical change. But in reality it’s going to be a slow, painful, uncertain transition. For both countries. Which begs the question: When a middle power cuts off its only superpower customer, which side runs out of money first? Despite its much smaller size, Canada does have some leverage. The U.S. needs Canadian energy, and Canadian minerals are critical for the U.S.’s defense industry. The integrated supply chains would take years to untangle. And the pain would ripple across on both sides of the border. But Canada is the smaller economy and therefore the one with more to lose. It's the one that will have to build enormous domestic capacity in sectors that have been neglected for decades.

segments.titre: Buy Canadian vision and the risk of fading support
segments.resume: Carney's vision of buying Canadian steel, aluminum, lumber and workers is politically powerful but economically fraught, and it is unclear Canada has the time, capital and resilience to complete it. Analysts warn support could disappear as consequences sink in, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, through CEO Candace Laing, urges surgical retaliation rather than endless escalation.
segments.texte: Carney’s vision of “Buy Canadian” steel, aluminum, lumber, and workers is politically powerful. But it’s also economically fraught. It’s an inspiring goal. The question is whether Canada has the time, the capital, and the resilience to achieve it before the costs of decoupling break the country. Carney continues to enjoy broad support from Canadians. But political analysts warn that support could disappear as the consequences of the trade war sink in. That’s why the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has urged the Carney government to take a surgical approach to retaliation. “Businesses understand retaliation but don’t want to see endless escalation,” said CEO and President Candace Laing.

segments.titre: Endless escalation and the slow collapse of US defense hegemony
segments.resume: The trade war, already 18 months old, keeps escalating, with the beginnings of US defense dominance cracking underneath. The narrator describes a grinding realignment rather than a sudden collapse: the EU steering budgets toward European weapons, Gulf States doubting US protection against Iranian missiles, and Carney's 70 cents declaration as a symptom, not the cause.
segments.texte: But endless escalation is what’s happening. Tariffs upon tariffs. Threats of further tariffs. A trade war that has already lasted 18 months and shows no sign of ending. And underneath it all, the beginnings of the U.S. defense dominance cracking. The collapse of American defense hegemony won’t happen in a single, sudden event. The U.S. military has been too powerful for too long, and too deeply embedded globally to just disappear overnight. It’ll be a grinding realignment driven by forces that no single leader can control. It’s happening in Europe. The EU is steering military budgets towards European weapons systems, instead of American hardware. Gulf States are realizing the U.S. can’t protect them from Iranian missiles the way they thought. And it’s being seen in Carney’s tough stance. His 70 cents declaration is a symptom of that slow collapse, not the cause. It’s a political response to a geopolitical reality. From Canada’s perspective, the U.S. is no longer a reliable ally and Canada must adapt. But that takes time. And time is the one resource Canada doesn’t have.

segments.titre: Conclusion: Canada trapped by its own declaration of independence
segments.resume: Integrated supply chains and decades of interdependence cannot be unwound with a rousing speech: Ontario and Quebec factories still need parts, pipelines still flow south and auto plants will stop under tariffs. Canada is trapped by its own declaration, and the only way out is years of economic suffering and difficult choices, with no one knowing how it ends.
segments.texte: The integrated supply chains, the shared infrastructure, the decades of economic interdependence can’t be unwound with a rousing speech. The applause in Montreal will fade. But the factories in Ontario and Quebec will still need parts. The pipelines will still flow south, even if they’re empty. And the auto plants will still stop production when tariffs make them unsustainable. Canada is trapped by its own declaration of independence. And the only way out is through years of economic suffering, strategic uncertainty, and difficult choices. The days of 70 cents of every dollar to the U.S. are over. A new geopolitical reality is dawning. And no one knows how this ends. But by the looks of things, it’s not going to end well.

segments.resume: Closing question about how both nations would respond if tensions really boiled over, with a pointer to the video 'Canada's Plan In Case of US Invasion' about how the Great White North could become an advantage.
